title: OpenTofu and the Terraform ecosystem choices
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: OpenTofu is an open source fork of Terraform, hosted by the Linux Foundation, started after Terraform moved to a source available licence.
For a given version range, the state format and configuration are largely compatible, which makes switching practical.
Examples are features added in only one project, different default registries and different licence terms for the tool itself.
Back up the state, pin the current tool version, run a plan with the current tool and save the output.
Pin the required version in code, avoid tool specific features in shared modules and run your CI against the versions you support.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A plan that wanted to replace a database
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
After switching tools, the first plan showed a destroy and create of a production database.
An operator runs a command such as: tofu plan -no-color | tail -4
The provider version was not pinned, so the new tool installed a newer provider that changed a default.
The team stopped before applying, pinned the provider to the previous version, saw a clean plan and scheduled the provider upgrade as its own change.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Switching tools and upgrading providers in one step.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Pulumi: infrastructure in real programming languages
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A Pulumi program declares resources and the engine compares them with the state of a stack, then creates, updates or deletes what differs.
A resource is an object created from a provider class.
Some values are known only after a resource exists, so Pulumi wraps them as outputs.
Mark values as secrets with `pulumi config set --secret` and the state stores them encrypted.
Code shines for repeated patterns, validation and tests with ordinary test frameworks.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: An output used before it existed
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A script printed a bucket name that never worked in a connection string.
An operator runs a command such as: pulumi stack output bucketUrl
The program built the URL by joining plain strings with the output object, which produced an unresolved placeholder in the application.
Using apply to build the string after the value existed fixed it, and a unit test now checks the final value.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Treating outputs as plain strings.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Terragrunt, modules and multi-environment structure
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A module is a reusable unit such as a network or a database.
One huge state means every plan reads everything and a mistake can touch everything.
Terragrunt is a thin wrapper that generates backend and provider configuration, passes inputs from a hierarchy of files and runs several stacks in order.
A stack often needs outputs from another, such as the network id.
Change a module in a branch, release a tag, then update the version in dev, then staging and then production, reading the plan each time.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A single apply that touched everything
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A change to a tag in a shared network stack planned changes for 400 resources.
An operator runs a command such as: terragrunt run-all plan --terragrunt-non-interactive 2>&1 | grep -c "will be updated in-place"
All environments pointed to the unversioned main branch of the module, so a one line change affected every stack at once.
The team pinned module versions by tag, promoted them through dev and staging and split the network stack so a change touches fewer resources.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Pointing modules at a branch instead of a tag.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Testing infrastructure code
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Cheap fast checks run on every commit, medium checks run on every pull request and expensive tests run on a schedule or before a release.
Use `fmt -check`, `validate` and a linter such as tflint to catch syntax errors, unused variables and invalid instance types.
Scan plans or code with tools such as Checkov, Trivy or a policy engine to find open security groups, unencrypted storage and public buckets before anything is created.
Terraform and OpenTofu support test files with run blocks and assertions.
Tools such as Terratest deploy real resources, check them and destroy them.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A test environment left running for a month
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
An integration test failed midway and left a database and a load balancer running.
An operator runs a command such as: aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources --tag-filters Key=env,Values=test --query 'ResourceTagMappingList[]
The test destroyed resources only on success.
Cleanup now runs in a final step that always executes, tests tag everything with an owner and expiry, and a nightly job deletes anything past its expiry in the test account.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Running only manual plans.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Policy as code and drift detection
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Good policies are specific and explainable: storage must be encrypted, only approved regions and instance sizes are allowed, public access needs an approval tag, every resource has an owner tag and cost centre.
A plan can be exported as JSON, and a policy engine such as Open Policy Agent with Conftest evaluates rules against it.
Run policy on every pull request so the author sees failures early, and run it again before apply.
Drift happens when someone changes a resource in the console or another tool.
If the change was wrong, apply the code to revert it and find out why access allowed it.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A security group opened in the console
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
During an incident someone opened a port to the internet and never closed it.
An operator runs a command such as: terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -no-color | tail -5
The nightly drift plan reported the change and a ticket was opened automatically.
The team reverted the rule through code, reviewed who could edit security groups in the console and added a policy that denies public ingress without an approved tag.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Policies nobody can explain.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: State, secrets and safe migrations
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Store state in a remote backend such as an object store with versioning, encryption and a lock table, so only one apply runs at a time and you can roll back a bad write.
Do not put secrets in code or variable files in the repository.
When you rename a resource or move it into a module, the tool sees a delete and a create.
To bring an existing resource under management, write the resource block and use an `import` block or the import command with its id.
To stop managing something without deleting it, use a `removed` block with `lifecycle { destroy = false }` or the state remove command.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A rename that planned to delete the database
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A refactor into modules changed resource addresses and the plan showed a destroy.
An operator runs a command such as: terraform plan -no-color | grep -E "destroyed|created" | head -3
The code moved the resource into a module without a moved block.
The team added a moved block from the old to the new address, the next plan showed only a move, and prevent_destroy was added to the database as a guard.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Renaming resources without moved blocks.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.
